<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" />{{rh|{{sc|Cha. V.}}|{{sc|according to s. marke.}}|99}}</noinclude>{{verse|chapter=5|verse=21}} {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Mat. 9, 18. Luc. 8, 42.''}}* And vvhen {{sc|Iesvs}} had pa{{ls}}{{ls}}ed in boate againe ouer the {{ls}}traite, a great multitude a{{ls}}{{ls}}embled together vnto him, and he vvas about the {{ls}}ea. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=22}} And there commeth one of the {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ ''Arch{{ls}}ynagogue'', cheefe gouerner of a Synagogue.}}∷ Arch{{ls}}ynagogs, named Iaîrus: and {{ls}}eeing him, he falleth dovvne at his feete, {{verse|chapter=5|verse=23}} and be{{ls}}ought him much, {{ls}}aying, That my daughter is at the point of death, come, impo{{ls}}e thy hands vpon her, that {{ls}}he may be {{ls}}afe and liue. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=24}} And he vvent vvith him, and a great multitude folovved him, and they thronged him.

{{verse|chapter=5|verse=25}} And a vvoman vvhich vvas in an i{{ls}}{{ls}}ue of bloud tvvelue yeres, {{verse|chapter=5|verse=26}} and had {{ls}}uffred many things of many Phy{{ls}}icions, and had be{{ls}}tovved al that {{ls}}he had, neither vvas any thing the better, but vvas rather vvor{{ls}}e: {{verse|chapter=5|verse=27}} vvhen {{ls}}he had heard of {{sc|Iesvs}}, {{ls}}he came in the prea{{ls}}{{ls}}e behind him, and touched his garment. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=28}} for {{ls}}he {{ls}}aid, That {{sup|‖}} if I {{ls}}hal touche but his garment, I {{ls}}hal be {{ls}}afe. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=29}} And forthvvith the fountaine of her bloud vvas dried: and {{ls}}he felt in her body that {{ls}}he vvas healed of the maladie. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=30}} And immediatly {{sc|Iesvs}} knovving in him {{ls}}elf the {{sup|‖}} vertue that had proceeded from him, turning to the multitude, {{ls}}aid, Who hath touched my garments? {{verse|chapter=5|verse=31}} And his Di{{ls}}ciples {{ls}}aid to him, Thou {{ls}}ee{{ls}}t the multitude thronging thee, and {{ls}}aye{{ls}}t thou, Who hath touched me? {{verse|chapter=5|verse=32}} And he looked about to {{ls}}ee her that had done this. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=33}} But the vvoman fearing and trembling, knovving vvhat vvas done in her: came and fel dovvne before him, and told him al the truth. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=34}} And he {{ls}}aid to her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee {{ls}}afe, goe in peace, and be vvhole of thy maladie.

{{verse|chapter=5|verse=35}} As he vvas yet {{ls}}peaking, they come {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''`from''}}`to' the Arch{{ls}}ynagogue, {{ls}}aying, That thy daughter is dead: vvhy doe{{ls}}t thou trouble the Mai{{ls}}ter any further? {{verse|chapter=5|verse=36}} But {{sc|Iesvs}} hauing heard the vvord that vvas {{ls}}poken, {{ls}}aith to the Arch{{ls}}ynagogue, Feare not: {{sup|‖}} only beleeue. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=37}} And he admitted not any man to folovv him, but Peter and Iames and Iohn the brother of Iames. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=38}} And they come to the Arch{{ls}}ynagogs hou{{ls}}e, and he {{ls}}eeth a tumult, and folke vveeping and vvailing much. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=39}} And going in, he {{ls}}aith to them: Why make you this a doe and vveepe? the vvenche is not dead, but {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ To Chri{{ls}}t, that can more ea{{ls}}ily rai{{ls}}e a dead man then we can doe one that is but a {{ls}}leepe, death is but {{ls}}leepe. ''Aug. de verb. Do. Ser. 44''.}}∷ {{ls}}leepeth. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=40}} And they derided him. But he hauing put forth al, taketh the father and the mother of the vvenche, and them that vvere vvith him, and they goe in vvhere the vvenche vvas lying. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=41}} And holding the vvenches hand, he {{ls}}aith to her, ''Talitha cumi'', vvhich is being interpreted, {{sup|‖}} ''wenche'' (I {{ls}}ay to thee) ''ari{{ls}}e''. {{verse|chapter=5|verse=42}} and {{hws|forth|forthvvith|title=forthvvith}}<noinclude>{{continues|vvith}}</noinclude>
